claims.text: A single or falling CRP result cannot exclude early-onset sepsis or alone determine whether antibiotics should stop. Clinical decisions regarding antibiotic initiation, continuation, or cessation must not rely solely on C-reactive protein results.

The decision to stop antibiotics at 36 hours for babies treated for early-onset infection risk factors requires a negative blood culture, low initial clinical suspicion, a reassuring clinical condition with no indicators of infection, and reassuring CRP levels and trends. The current patient has an unknown culture status and undocumented red flags, meaning these criteria are not yet fully met.

CRP levels and trends are a component of the assessment for antibiotic review but are not sufficient on their own. For this patient, CRP has decreased from 18 to 9 to 3 mg/L over 6 hours. While this trend is part of the data, it must be interpreted alongside clinical progress and culture results to determine if the levels are 'reassuring' in the context of stopping therapy.

If antibiotics are continued beyond 48 hours for suspected infection despite a negative blood culture, the baby must be reviewed at least once every 24 hours. At each review, the decision to stop antibiotics must account for the initial clinical suspicion, the baby's current clinical progress and condition, and the levels and trends of CRP.

For babies with strong initial clinical suspicion of infection who require antibiotics for more than 36 hours despite a negative blood culture, consideration may be given to switching from intravenous to oral antibiotics at 36 hours or later to complete the course, provided the clinical condition is reassuring, CRP trends are reassuring, and the baby is tolerating oral feeds.

evidence.text: If continuing antibiotics for longer than 48 hours for suspected late‑onset neonatal infection despite negative blood culture, review the baby at least once every 24 hours. At each review, decide whether to stop antibiotics, taking account of: • the level of initial clinical suspicion of infection and • the baby's clinical progress and current condition and • the levels and trends of C-reactive protein. [2021]

For babies who are being treated with intravenous antibiotics because of risk factors for early-onset infection or clinical indicators of possible infection, stop antibiotics at 36 hours if: • the blood culture is negative and • the initial clinical suspicion of infection was not strong and • the baby's clinical condition is reassuring, with no clinical indicators of possible infection (see box 2 for clinical indicators of possible early-onset infection) and • the levels and trends of C-reactive protein concentration are reassuring. [2012, amended 2026]

For babies born from 35+0 weeks' gestation with negative blood culture who need antibiotics for more than 36 hours because the initial clinical suspicion of infection was strong, consider switching treatment from intravenous to oral antibiotics at 36 hours or thereafter to complete the course (up to 7 days of antibiotics in total) if: • the baby's clinical condition is reassuring, with no current clinical indicators of ongoing infection (see box 2 for clinical indicators of possible early-onset neonatal infection) and • the levels and trends of C-reactive protein concentration are reassuring and • the baby is tolerating oral feeds. [2026]
Do not use C-reactive protein results alone to make decisions about starting, continuing or stopping antibiotics. [2026]
